new_entities.name: Early-life vitamin D exposure
aliases: prenatal or infant vitamin D supplementation
new_entities.description: Vitamin D supplementation or status during pregnancy, infancy, or very early childhood.

edges.effect_quant: The early-life vitamin D literature is mostly a null or selective-signal story: little consistent effect on the overall allergic-disease bundle, with some narrower hints for reduced wheeze or eczema in specific contexts.
edges.population: pregnant women, infants, and children exposed to higher vitamin D intake or status early in life
edges.mechanism: Vitamin D shapes epithelial barrier function and immune differentiation, so a prevention signal is biologically plausible. The problem is that human studies do not translate that plausibility into a strong, broad reduction in allergic outcomes.
edges.summary: This edge should not be oversold. The most current syntheses show little consistent effect of early-life vitamin D on the broad allergic-disease package, although some sub-analyses hint at lower wheeze or eczema risk in narrower settings.
edges.caveats: This is a heterogeneous literature mixing prenatal supplementation, infant supplementation, cord-blood status, and dietary intake. Those are not interchangeable exposures, so a broad null-to-mixed label is more defensible than a confident protective claim.

evidence.citation: Zeng R et al 2023 Clin Exp Allergy
evidence.notes: Is antenatal or early-life vitamin D associated with eczema or food allergy in childhood? A systematic review.
